articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
In a bit of a late-August surprise while the world awaits word on the next generation of iPhones, on Tuesday Apple announced two new processors, the M5 Ultra and M6, which help power new iterations of its Mac Studio and Mac mini desktop computers. Both models are available to pre-order now and will ship on September 22 and will run macOS 27 Golden Gate.

Bridging the generations

The M6 chip kicks off Apple’s next chip generation, and is its first based on a 2-nanometer production process. It’s also got the first 12-core CPU in Apple’s base M-series chip line, up from 10 cores in the M4 and M5 generations.

Those CPU cores are in an interesting configuration: The M6 is the first Apple chip to mix all three of its CPU core types. The chip has six efficiency cores, four performance cores, and two super cores.

According to Apple, each core design is focused on a different primary task: efficiency cores are meant to sip power (useful when running simple background tasks); performance cores are optimized for complex, multi-threaded jobs; and super cores were created to offer the highest possible single-threaded performance.

Apple claims that this design results in record-setting single-threaded performance and up to 1.2x speed improvements over the M5 chip. The M6 also offers a dual 16-core Neural Engine, for on-device AI performance. Memory bandwidth peaks at 170GB/s, 10 percent faster than the M5.

Just as the new chip generation arrives, the previous one ( launched in October 2025 ) is completed. The M5 Ultra is Apple’s first new Ultra chip since it introduced the M3 Ultra in March 2025. Apple says it’s using the next generation of its UltraFusion technology to connect two dual-die M5 Max chips to make Apple silicon’s first quad-die chip. UltraFusion connects the two dies with bandwidth of more than 4.4TB/s, letting the four dies work as a single chip.

The M5 Ultra offers up to 36 CPU cores (12 super/24 performance), which Apple says results in up to 1.25x higher single-threaded performance and up to 1.3x higher multithreaded performance than the M3 Ultra. It offers up to 80 GPU cores and up to 512GB of memory with 1.2TB/s of unified memory bandwidth.

Meet the Mac mini

Previously available in M4 and M4 Pro configurations, the new Mac mini is available in M6 and M5 Pro chip options. The new base price is $899, up $100 from the previous base, for the same standard 16GB RAM/256GB storage configuration. The M5 Pro configuration starts at $1699, also up $100 from the model sold until Tuesday.

(But keep in mind, the M4 Mac mini was introduced at $599 before Apple recently raised that price. Put together, it’s a 50% price increase over the model introduced almost two years ago. We all know why, but it still hurts. )

Because the Mac mini previously shipped with M4 processors, this new model picks up numerous improvements Apple made in the M5 generation, including GPUs better optimized for AI performance. Both models support Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 via Apple’s N1 chip, and 2.5Gb Ethernet is now standard, with 10Gb Ethernet still available as an add-on. The M6 model supports Thunderbolt 4, but the M5 Pro model supports Thunderbolt 5.

Mac Studio advances in unison

At the same moment the Mac mini becomes split between two chip generations, the Mac Studio gets reunified with chips from the same generation: the M5 Max and the new M5 Ultra. As mentioned previously, the M5 Ultra is basically two M5 Max chips connected together by Apple’s dense, fast UltraFusion technology. Apple boasts that the M5 Ultra is the fastest chip Apple has ever created, which isn’t much of a stretch since the M5 Max was already pretty far up there.

The Mac Studio is effectively the replacement for the Mac Pro, and it’s alone in offering the Ultra-class chip. Apple has positioned the Mac Studio as ideal for local AI workflows, and the new models will still be able to cluster via Thunderbolt 5 to create even larger collections of memory and performance.

Apple representatives pointed out that a four-Mac Studio AI cluster, like the one I saw on display at WWDC earlier this summer, is so efficient that it can be powered from a single standard wall outlet. (They even showed us a picture of four Mac Studios plugged into a power strip that was plugged into the wall.

) In an era of data center excesses, Apple is clearly leaning into the possibility of small, efficient Macs being used to do local AI work rather than relying on huge, power-hungry cloud models.

As with the Mac mini, the Mac Studio gains M5 chip improvements that benefit AI models running on GPU cores, integrate the N1 chip for Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, and support 2x faster storage with speeds up to 15GB/s.

articles.title: Hands-On with Computer History: OpenAI’s Take on Agent Memory
articles.subtitle: Late yesterday, OpenAI revealed the sort of automation catnip I love: Computer History. It’s a new feature for Pro, Business, and Enterprise subscribers that creates continuity for ChatGPT and Codex by converting the actions you take on your Mac into...
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Late yesterday, OpenAI revealed the sort of automation catnip I love: Computer History. It’s a new feature for Pro, Business, and Enterprise subscribers that creates continuity for ChatGPT and Codex by converting the actions you take on your Mac into Markdown memory files that serve as context for subsequent interactions.

The idea is that with the additional context, ChatGPT and Codex will better understand your requests, requiring you to provide less detail up front while getting better results. Anyone familiar with OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, and similar projects will know where this is going.

Here’s how it works.

Computer History is currently a Mac-only feature that is turned off by default, so if you want to try it, head to the Integrations section of the desktop app’s settings and toggle it on. History entries can be cleared individually, too. Before you get started, ChatGPT explains that you can pause or clear your history and manage the apps and websites that Computer History accesses at any time.

I excluded Passwords, 1Password, and Keychain Access to start and may add to that list as I use the feature more and get a better sense for the sort of information that it collects.

That opening alert also says you agree to pause Computer History during video and audio calls with others to avoid recording them without their consent. I appreciate the reminder that recording people without consent is something you shouldn’t do and is even illegal in some places, but as with the many meeting summarization tools on the market, I doubt that very many people will heed the warning and comply even though doing so is just a click of the menu bar away.

Still, I appreciate the alert up front, because turning Computer History on requires trust that the information won’t be misused by OpenAI. I’m sure that’s a bridge too far for some, but one of the most frustrating parts of using a tool like Codex is explaining yourself over and over. Every thread is like Groundhog Day for an agent, and while there are techniques that help provide continuity, making it automatic with Computer History is an exciting prospect.

If you’re intrigued by the potential, it pays to read OpenAI’s documentation and understand how the feature works. First of all, Computer History is not the same as Chronicle, a retired research preview feature that relied on taking screenshots as you worked.

In contrast, Computer History records interaction events but not screenshots, audio, or private web browsing sessions, according to OpenAI’s documentation. In practice, what that means is that as you work, ChatGPT will record your switches from app to app and what you’re doing in apps. Here’s what it’s captured as I started work on this story:

As you can see, every 10 minutes, ChatGPT creates a brief, timestamped summary of what I’ve been doing and lists the apps I’ve used by their icons. If I hover over an entry, I can immediately delete it or open the source file in the Finder for more detail on the information that ChatGPT is collecting.

Each entry in Computer History is a Markdown file with YAML front matter that includes a title, description, and list of the apps you’ve used followed by a structured memory document. Here, you’ll see a summary of what you’ve done:

The user continued writing computer history. md in Obsidian’s MacStories Vault, refining the section that explains how Computer History differs from the earlier Chronicle preview and adding a practical description of what the feature records while the user works.

The user referenced the OpenAI Learn Computer History documentation in Safari, briefly exchanged messages with Federico Viticci, checked ChatGPT/Codex settings, and then opened MacStories Images to queue a screenshot named CleanShot 2026-08-14 at 06. 08. 44@2x. png for upload. The upload was queued by the end of the segment, but no completed upload or copied Markdown image link was observed.

You’ll also find details that ChatGPT deems important and non-obvious, such as the following:

articles.title: Apple’s new Foundation Models explained: on-device AI, cloud AI, and everything in between
articles.subtitle: During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips. Here’s a breakdown of how that will work.

A bit of background

When Apple first announced its foundation models in 2024, the lineup included an on-device language model with roughly 3 billion parameters, and “a larger server-based language model available with Private Cloud Compute and running on Apple silicon servers,” as the company put it at the time.

Private Cloud Compute was an ambitious undertaking, as it aimed to deliver cloud-based AI capabilities while preserving the same privacy guarantees users expect from on-device processing.

For this reason, keeping everything in-house was essential. Private Cloud Compute ran in Apple data centers, on servers powered by Apple silicon. Even so, its privacy guarantees could be independently verified by third-party security researchers.

However, as Apple struggled to get its AI aspirations off the ground, the company partnered with Google to use Gemini as the backbone of its new AI efforts, the results of which it announced earlier this week during the WWDC26 keynote.

Apple’s new foundation models

The third generation of AFMs includes five models: AFM 3 Core and AFM 3 Code Advanced, which are on-device models, and AFM Cloud, ADM 3 Cloud (Image), and AFM 3 Cloud Pro, which are server-based. The D in ADM 3 Cloud (Image) stands for diffusion, a technology we’ve covered in the past here.

Except for AFM 3 Cloud Pro, all other models were built to run on Apple silicon devices. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, meanwhile, runs on NVIDIA GPUs hosted in Google Cloud.

This was made possible afer Apple extended its Private Cloud Compute architecture to third-party infrastructure for the first time, “while maintaining Apple’s powerful security and privacy protections,” according to the company.

As for the models themselves, here’s a breakdown of each one, as explained by Apple:

AFM 3 Core, the next generation of our 3-billion-parameter dense model that delivers a step up in quality. AFM 3 Core Advanced, our most powerful on-device model. It’s natively multimodal, enabling helpful features like expressive voices and higher-accuracy dictation.

Built on cutting-edge Apple research, this 20-billion-parameter model uses a sparse architecture, activating just 1 to 4 billion parameters at a time depending on the request. AFM 3 Core Advanced is unlocked by and optimized for our most capable Apple silicon systems. AFM 3 Cloud, our server-side workhorse, optimized for speed, efficiency, and performance.

ADM 3 Cloud (Image), for image generation and editing, which unlocks advanced photo-editing tools, the all-new Image Playground, and more. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, our most capable server-based model, which powers our most demanding use cases, like agentic tool use and complex reasoning.

articles.title: New Game of Thrones Official Release Will Let Fans Rewrite Canon
articles.subtitle: Classic real-time strategy game War for Westeros is giving strong Battle for Middle-earth vibes The war for Westeros is about to change.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Classic real-time strategy game War for Westeros is giving strong Battle for Middle-earth vibes

The war for Westeros is about to change. On Tuesday at Gamescom Opening Night Live, developer PlaySide Studios revealed the first gameplay trailer for Game of Thrones: War for Westeros, showing how the factions of the Seven Kingdoms will battle for control of the Iron Throne.

In a new Gamescom gameplay trailer, Playside's classic real-time strategy game looks to appeal to both Game of Thrones fans and devotees of games like Warcraft 3 and The Lord of the Rings: The Battle for Middle-earth, with hero characters leading battalions in bloody battle to control castles and land.

How does Game of Thrones: War for Westeros play?

War for Westeros will give players command of multiple familiar factions, including House Stark, House Lannister, House Targaryen, and the Night King's White Walkers, to conquer the Seven Kingdoms and decide who sits the Iron Throne. The game's various armies will be led by playable heroes, including Robb Stark, Jon Snow, Ghost, Grey Wind, Jaime Lannister, Tywin Lannister, Daenerys Targaryen, and the Night King. Each hero has their own unique abilities.

"Forging a path to victory will require players to step into the role of a commander, making key decisions in training units, securing resources, constructing buildings, and claiming territory from opposing forces," Playside said in a news release. "Each faction offers asymmetric strategies, with unique armies, buildings, mechanics, and playstyles shaped by their identity in the Game of Thrones series.

Players must harness these distinct strengths, deploy powerful heroes, and adapt their approach to outplay, outmaneuver, and defeat their enemies. "

Ultimately, it appears that players will be able to change the course of the events of Game of Thrones in War for Westeros, so if you ever wanted to give Jaime Lannister a better death than he got on screen, this is your chance.

Image: Playside Studios

Game of Thrones: War for Westeros is coming in early 2027 to Windows PC via Steam.

Fans who have finished House of the Dragon and A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms have something new to look forward to

articles.title: Apple Introduces Two New Groundbreaking Chips: M6 and M5 Ultra
articles.subtitle: Apple today capped off one generation of Apple Silicon while launching another. And both new chips are important in their own way.
articles.author: OWC Rocket Yard
articles.content:
Apple today capped off one generation of Apple Silicon while launching another. And both new chips are important in their own way. The new M6 represents a leap forward in chip architecture while the new M5 Ultra is the most powerful chip the company has produced to date.

Let’s take a deeper look at the purpose behind these chips and the performance gains you can expect to see.

M6: Small Chip, Big Jump

The M6 is a big deal because it’s the very first 2-nanometer (nm) chip to hit the market. Without getting too technical, as we have gone from 5nm chips to 3nm chips and now to 2nm, what that translates to is Apple’s ability to pack more transistors onto a chip. That translates to faster speeds with less heat being generated for improved sustained performance.

The M6 packs a 12-core CPU — two cores more than M5 — split into 2 “super cores,” 4 performance cores, and 6 efficiency cores. An additional two cores on a base model chip is a big deal and Apple says the super cores in particular deliver the fastest single-threaded performance of any CPU core on the market. Meanwhile, multithreaded gains reach up to 1. 2x over M5 and 2. 4x over the original M1.

In other words, if you’re still holding on to an M1- or even M2-generation Mac, you will see performance improvements with M6 that will be very, very noticeable.

M6’s new 12-core GPU adds a Neural Accelerator to every core, boosting peak AI compute by nearly 30 percent over M5 and more than 8x over M1. These gains translate to noticeably snappier on-device LLM prompt processing. On the gaming/graphics side, M6 brings Dynamic Caching, hardware-accelerated ray tracing, and a 50 percent bump in geometry rates.

Rounding things out, M6 introduces a Dual 16-core Neural Engine that doubles peak AI compute versus M5, with system frameworks able to tap both engines at once for faster model execution.

Like the M5, M6 unified memory support tops out at 32GB though bandwidth has climbed 10 percent to 170GB/s.

M5 Ultra: Beastly New Quad-Die Architecture

Apple introduced its Fusion Architecture technology earlier this year with the launch of the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips. On those chips, the process fuses together two third-generation 3-nanometer dies into single a chip package with high bandwidth and low latency. The reason that’s important context is that it laid the groundwork for what Apple just announced for M5 Ultra.

Ultra chips have always been two chips fused together using a process Apple calls UltraFusion. So, when Apple launched the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips as single chips formed by fusing multiple dies, it was reasonable to assume that the next Ultra chips would then fuse two of those double-die chips together as well to create an absolute behemoth of a chip.

And that’s exactly what happened with M5 Ultra. If you’re following our math, that makes M5 Ultra the first Apple chip to fuse four dies together using an upgraded generation of of UltraFusion. We used to get excited about quad core processors. Now Apple is producing quad-die processors. And if you’re going to fuse four dies together, you’ve got to be able to support a lot of bandwidth.

UltraFusion’s inter-die bandwidth now exceeds 4. 4TB/s, with connection density up more than 6x, letting the four dies act as one unified chip rather than a cluster of separate parts.

The resulting spec sheet is staggering: up to a 36-core CPU (12 super cores plus 24 performance cores) delivering up to 1.25x faster single-threaded and 1.3x faster multithreaded performance than M3 Ultra, alongside an up-to-80-core GPU that Apple says offers 4.5x the peak AI compute of M3 Ultra and more than 6x that of the original M1 Ultra. Every one of those GPU cores includes a Neural Accelerator, and the chip pairs all of that with a 32-core Neural Engine for on-device AI tasks.

Then there’s memory. M5 Ultra supports up to 512GB of unified memory with an absolutely massive 1.2TB/s of bandwidth. That’s 50 percent higher than M3 Ultra and enough, Apple says, to keep enormous datasets and LLMs with hundreds of billions of parameters entirely in local memory, no cloud round-trip required. As we covered in our primer to running local AI models on a Mac, these M5 Ultra numbers represent the ability to run multiple extremely capable local models.

Raising the Roof—and the Floor

These chips represent major advances at both the entry-level end of the Mac lineup and at the high-end. The M6 launches inside the new Mac mini while the M5 Ultra is available in the latest Mac Studio. You can read more about the new Mac mini here and more about the new Mac Studio here.

Apple Unveils M6 and M5 Ultra Chips With Huge CPU, GPU and AI Upgrades

Apple has introduced the new M6 Mac mini with a faster processor, improved graphics, higher memory bandwidth, faster storage, and upgraded wireless connectivity. The compact desktop keeps the same 5-inch design introduced with the M4 generation, so nearly all of the meaningful changes are inside the machine.

The M6 Mac mini starts at $899 with 16GB of unified memory and 256GB of SSD storage, while the previous M4 model originally launched at $599 with the same base memory and storage capacities. Apple is taking pre-orders for the new model now, with availability starting September 22.

M6 Mac mini vs M4 Mac mini specifications

M6 brings a 12-core CPU and Apple’s first 2nm design

The largest upgrade comes from the M6 chip, which moves to a 2nm manufacturing process and increases the CPU from 10 cores on M4 to 12 cores. Apple has also changed the CPU configuration, using two super cores, four performance cores, and six efficiency cores.

Set us as a preferred source and our Apple reporting ranks higher in your Google Search results and Discover feed — one tap, no account changes.

Apple says the M6 Mac mini delivers up to 40 percent faster CPU performance than the M4 generation. The additional cores should provide the biggest improvement in sustained multithreaded workloads such as code compilation, video processing, software development, and other CPU-heavy tasks.

The M4 uses four performance cores and six efficiency cores, giving it 10 CPU cores in total, alongside 120GB/s of unified memory bandwidth.

GPU performance gets a much larger upgrade

The M6 includes a 12-core GPU compared with the M4’s 10-core GPU, but the architectural changes matter more than the additional two cores. Each M6 GPU core includes a Neural Accelerator designed to accelerate AI workloads directly through the graphics architecture.

Apple says graphics rendering with ray tracing can run up to twice as fast as on the M4 in some games. This should also benefit GPU-heavy creative applications, 3D rendering, image processing, and workloads that use machine learning alongside traditional graphics processing.

articles.title: Surprise report: New Mac mini could land any day now
articles.subtitle: Macworld Apple may yet spring one final surprise of the Tim Cook era, with a new report raising hopes that the company plans to launch an updated version of the Mac mini “as soon as the coming days.” (Update: it’s now been announced.) Writing for...
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
Apple may yet spring one final surprise of the Tim Cook era, with a new report raising hopes that the company plans to launch an updated version of the Mac mini “as soon as the coming days.” (Update: it’s now been announced.)

Writing for Bloomberg, well-connected leaker Mark Gurman says Apple is gearing up to unveil the first new Mac mini in almost two years. He bases this on the testimony of unnamed sources “familiar with the matter.”

The last Mac mini model, announced on October 29, 2024, featured a major redesign (it was significantly smaller than its predecessor) as well as a faster M4 chip. This machine has become extremely popular, Gurman says, for running AI applications, but the ongoing memory crunch means Apple has struggled to meet demand. The Mac mini has essentially been out of stock since the spring, with delivery times slipping into months-long waits.

That isn’t to say that Apple necessarily thinks the new model will help in this regard. Gurman acknowledges that it’s unclear “how the new model will affect wait times,” as an updated mini is unlikely to require less memory than the current one. It seems more likely that Apple simply feels it’s time for an update, and the product’s popularity has pushed it to the front of the line.

Gurman’s report is generally short on details, with little information offered regarding design (although we can guess that another redesign would be a surprise so soon after the last one) and tech specs, where he says only that models with both M5 and M6 chips have been tested. The main takeaway regards timings.

Gurman says the new Mac mini could arrive ahead of the iPhone Ultra and iPhone 18 Pro, which will appear in early September and likely on September 9, and even says it will likely be the last product to launch under Cook’s watch.

Cook is slated to exit the CEO seat on September 1, which (assuming Gurman’s speculation is correct) gives a window of just seven days for the Mac mini to arrive. And we can rule out most of those days because they’re unsuitable for an announcement; by far the most plausible are Tuesday and Wednesday of this week. It could launch today, in other words.

The mini is only one of the Macs getting an update this fall as part of a massive overhaul. For all the latest news and rumors, bookmark our regularly updated new Mac mini superguide.

articles.subtitle: OpenAI is giving ChatGPT and Codex a new way to learn from and remember how you use your Mac, even when that work happens outside the app.

articles.content:
OpenAI is giving ChatGPT and Codex a new way to learn from and remember how you use your Mac, even when that work happens outside the app.

ChatGPT Computer History is an upgraded replacement for Codex’s Chronicle research preview

The new Computer History feature builds a searchable timeline from activity across selected apps and websites.

OpenAI announced Computer History in Thursday’s desktop app changelog. The feature is off by default and must be enabled by each user, giving people control over which sources contribute to their history.

The release comes a month after Codex joined ChatGPT on the desktop. It also follows OpenAI’s experimental Chronicle feature from earlier this year.

OpenAI says Computer History actually replaces the Chronicle research preview, but calls it a rebuilt system rather than a simple rename.

Chronicle relied on screenshots. Computer History instead records interaction events exposed through macOS accessibility features, including clicks, typing, keyboard shortcuts, and switching between apps.

Here’s how OpenAI describes the new feature:

Computer History is an opt-in feature in the ChatGPT desktop app on macOS that turns activity across apps and websites into memories and a timeline that ChatGPT and Codex can use. Choose which apps and websites contribute, pause collection, and review or delete your history at any time. Computer History is available to ChatGPT Pro, Business, and Enterprise users.

Computer History is off by default for ChatGPT Pro, Business, and Enterprise users in the ChatGPT desktop app on macOS. Pro users can choose to turn it on. For Business and Enterprise workspaces, an administrator must explicitly grant access before each member can choose to turn it on.

articles.title: Craig Federighi and Greg Joswiak talk Siri AI and more in new interview [Video]
articles.subtitle: On the heels of Apple’s WWDC keynote this week, Greg Joswiak and Craig Federighi sat down with Laurie Segall on the Mostly Human podcast.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
On the heels of Apple’s WWDC keynote this week, Greg Joswiak and Craig Federighi sat down with Laurie Segall on the Mostly Human podcast. During the conversation, Federighi and Joz talked in-depth about Apple’s new Siri AI and Apple Intelligence announcements, the company’s broader approach to AI, and more.

I really enjoyed this explanation from Federighi about Apple’s approach to AI and why he thinks it’s totally reasonable that some people are spooked by how fast things are moving right now:

I think that AI, in Apple’s view, can be used as this incredibly empowering thing. But there is a sense that, for one, things are changing very fast in ways that I think it’s hard for any normal person to keep up with. There’s uncertainty about where does this all lead?

And while I think we can look at this as yet another thing of the scale of the Industrial Revolution, which changed our world in a giant way, that displaced a lot of people in the process and still occurred over like 80 years. And now this is happening in a compressed time frame. And so I think it’s fair for people to say, “Wow, I’m not quite certain what this is going to mean for me.

” And if you’re a student and you’re thinking, “Did I study the right thing? Is the job that I thought was the skill that I thought was going to be useful? Is that the one that’s going to be useful now that AI is quickly learning all of these things? ” I think those are all reasonable thoughts to have. You know, we’re in California. We’re optimists.

We’re trying to do the right thing where we can play the right role in our sense. And I do think in the end, this all has a happy ending, but I can certainly relate to people who say, “Wow, this is a big change. ” I mean, honestly, at this moment in time, there’s no bigger place where there’s that change than in software engineering.

It’s literally the first job that AI is showing that it can do to an incredible degree. And so everyone who works in my organization is saying, “Wow, this thing does a lot of things that I used to take a lot of pride in spending decades learning to do well, and it already does it well. Is the job that I thought was the skill that I thought was going to be useful?

Is that the one that’s going to be useful now that AI is quickly learning all of these things? ” I think those are all reasonable thoughts to have.

I think that AI, in Apple’s view, can be used as this incredibly empowering thing. But there is a sense that, for one, things are changing very fast in ways that I think it’s hard for any normal person to keep up with. There’s uncertainty about where does this all lead?

And while I think we can look at this as yet another thing of the scale of the Industrial Revolution, which changed our world in a giant way, that displaced a lot of people in the process and still occurred over like 80 years.

And now this is happening in a compressed time frame. And so I think it’s fair for people to say, “Wow, I’m not quite certain what this is going to mean for me.”

And if you’re a student and you’re thinking, “Did I study the right thing? Is the job that I thought was the skill that I thought was going to be useful? Is that the one that’s going to be useful now that AI is quickly learning all of these things?”

I think those are all reasonable thoughts to have.

You know, we’re in California. We’re optimists. We’re trying to do the right thing where we can play the right role in our sense. And I do think in the end, this all has a happy ending, but I can certainly relate to people who say, “Wow, this is a big change.”

I mean, honestly, at this moment in time, there’s no bigger place where there’s that change than in software engineering. It’s literally the first job that AI is showing that it can do to an incredible degree.

And so everyone who works in my organization is saying, “Wow, this thing does a lot of things that I used to take a lot of pride in spending decades learning to do well, and it already does it well. Congrats to Tim Cook on his 15-year anniversary as CEO of Apple! Here are some balloons and a gift card to the Olive Garden. There will be cake in the break room.

It occurs to this furry observer that this is his last column before Tim Cook steps down as CEO of Apple. Hard to believe. The sad truth is that pretty soon we won’t have Tim Cook to kick around anymore. Other than the fact that he will still be working for the company, just in a different capacity, and we will absolutely still have him to kick around.

Still, it’s worth reviewing Cook’s tenure as Apple CEO. Apple loves it when you write reviews, right? So let’s get into it!

The Macalope’s not going to focus on politics. Apparently, there are some people who do not like it when the Macalope discusses politics.

That wouldn’t stop the horny one in any way from talking about it (it might even encourage him), but he thinks he’s already been clear about his feelings on Cook’s recent forays into the political world and Cook hasn’t done anything of late to really get the antlers itching, if you know what the Macalope means (you don’t and you do not want to). The Macalope has no idea what Cook’s personal politics are.

He suspects they probably pretty much align with his own. Cook’s business politics, however, would best be driven out to a rural town and gently tipped into an underground coal fire, never to be seen again.

So, it’s a little rich (allusion intended) when the Macalope sees things like this:

I hope that people say I was a good and decent man. And if they say that at the end of the day, I feel like I have achieved something. Apple CEO Tim Cook (CBS News interview, August 13, 2026)

I hope that people say I was a good and decent man. And if they say that at the end of the day, I feel like I have achieved something.

Mmm. Sorry, Tim. You might need a time machine for that.

But let’s just look at Cook’s legacy as a simple CEO running a small business in downtown Cupertino.

If you’re an Apple investor, it’s hard not to think of Cook as one of the greatest CEOs of all time. The Macalope’s not going to bother to look it up and figure it out with stock splits and buybacks and all the free coffee distributed and t-shirts shot out of a canon at shareholders meetings, but if you invested 15 years ago when Cook took over, you have to be happy with the returns.

(Hilariously, 15 years ago is about exactly when the Macalope sold the two (2) shares of Apple stock he owned.)

As someone who regularly had to deal with nincompoops who continued to say Apple was going to go out of business long after it made a lick of sense, the Macalope owes Cook a personal debt of gratitude for finally making it clear that that was not a thing you could say anymore and be taken seriously by anyone.

Despite the insistence of many that Apple hasn’t released any truly great products since Steve Jobs died, Apple has actually released some truly great products since Steve Jobs died. Sure, none of them have been as world-changing as the iPhone, the greatest consumer electronics product of all time, but, you know, that’s a pretty high bar. The Apple Watch, loudly declared a flop for years, is everywhere, as are AirPods, and Apple TV continues to churn out hit shows and movies.

articles.title: Big Walk: A Good Hang with Friends
articles.subtitle: I dove into Big Walk with no expectations at all. I’d seen trailers leading up to the launch and knew that it was a co-op puzzle game from House House, the makers of Untitled Goose Game, but that was about it.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
I dove into Big Walk with no expectations at all. I’d seen trailers leading up to the launch and knew that it was a co-op puzzle game from House House, the makers of Untitled Goose Game, but that was about it. And because most of my gaming is done solo, I initially tuned out most of the game’s post-launch headlines. Still, Big Walk is published by Panic, which has a great track record for finding and publishing great indie games, so I decided to give it a try earlier this week. And you know what? I love it.

Big Walk is about as low-key as a puzzle game gets in the best possible way. Co-op is the only mode, so you’ll need to coordinate a time to play it with a friend or group. One person takes the lead, setting up the session and inviting the others. The process is far simpler than trying to find a time that works for everyone in your group.

As players join, you’re dropped into a space to wait for the others and explore a little. This lobby space is where you’ll learn the game’s controls, too. Big Walk supports keyboard and mouse input as well as a controller, which is what I used, playing on an M4 Max MacBook Pro.

Once you get your bearings, it’s time to exit the lobby and start exploring. That exploration is core to what Big Walk is all about. You aren’t told what to do, but there are just enough clues to push you forward, figuring out the goals on your own without too much trouble.

I played using AirPods Pro 3, and the game made great use of their mics and speakers, simulating the environments we were in. Closed spaces were echoey, and speech was distant and faint when we were separated. Sound even becomes part of the mechanic in some puzzles, such as an early one where you have to look through an open window to hear each other properly and help guide the other player’s actions.

That cooperation is the key part of the game’s loop. You may see how to solve Big Walk’s puzzles on your own, but implementing the solution will require you and a companion to work together.

The togetherness of it all extends beyond the puzzles, too. Big Walk’s environment (at least in the early stages) is mountainous with large rocks and trees that make it possible to get separated from others. Add to that day and night cycles where it’s almost impossible to see where you’re going at night without a light, and you have every incentive not to wander off on your own without a plan for how to reconnect.

I’ve played through Big Walk’s first couple of sections, and it was a blast. The puzzles were clever and challenging without being frustrating, but most of all, I enjoyed working through them with someone else. There’s no time pressure or monsters lurking around corners – just puzzles and a chance to chat.

Ultimately, that’s what makes Big Walk work. It’s a good hang built against the backdrop of a beautiful landscape and low-key, fun challenges. I highly recommend giving it a try.

Big Walk, which supports crossplay and 2–12 players, is available on the Mac App Store for $14.99. The game is also on Steam, the Switch 2, and PS5.

Apple was roundly criticised back in 2024 for using concept videos of features it was unable to demo.

What Apple showed regarding the upcoming “personalized Siri” at WWDC was not a demo. It was a concept video. Concept videos are bullshit, and a sign of a company in disarray, if not crisis.

That criticism was deserved, and Apple admitted that things were going to take longer than expected, deleted the offending video, and settled a $250M false advertising lawsuit.

The company seems to have learned its lesson. While the keynote wasn’t live, it does appear that all of the video demonstrations were conducted in real time, as TechCrunch noted.

Many of the Apple Intelligence demoes featured someone standing, phone in hand, pressing buttons or using voice commands in real time, while another camera showed off the phone’s response. These weren’t live onstage, anything-could-go wrong demos; they were pre-taped. But they looked far more like proof of working features than what Apple showed at WWDC 2024.

Indeed, John Gruber observed that there weren’t even any cuts between individual demos.

The demos were all shot in single takes, with no editing. In fact, I think most of them were single takes of multiple demos back-to-back.

What Apple showed off, then, appears to be a genuine reflection of how the new AI features work today. Joz actually says that because the demos were filmed a little ahead of WWDC, they were carried out with an older version of Siri AI, and it’s faster now:

We actually filmed these a bit in advance, that was Siri AI where it was at that point. You ask those same questions to it now, it’ll be faster, and at launch it will be faster still.

articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
Plug your MacBook in and out of a multi-port laptop docking station to swiftly add multiple devices and external displays with just one cable connection to your laptop. We tested the top contenders to find the best Thunderbolt and USB-C docks available to owners of the MacBook Air and MacBook Pro. MacBook Neo users can use any of these docks but are limited to a 10Gbps bandwidth and some display limitations.

Thunderbolt, USB4 or USB-C

The connectors all look the same (technically known as a “Type-C connector”), but there are significant differences, particularly on speed that will determine both data-transfer rate and higher external display refresh rates.

USB-C: 5Gbps or 10Gbps

USB4: 20Gbps or 40Gbps

Thunderbolt 3 and 4: 40Gbps

Thunderbolt 5: 80Gbps / 120Gbps

Our list Which ports does my MacBook have will show you how many USB-C or more likely one of Thunderbolt 3, 4 or 5 that you have.

While a Thunderbolt 4 (TB4) dock will be enough for most casual users, if you can stretch the budget go for a TB5 dock as it will remain current for years, saving you money in the long term, and is backwards compatible with earlier versions and all the way back to USB-C. High-end professionals should always aim for Thunderbolt 5.

The dock needs one (“ upstream “) Thunderbolt or USB-C port for connecting to and charging your laptop (although all recent MacBooks can also power via the MagSafe 3 port), and at least another (“ downstream “) to attach further devices (hard drives, external display, and others).

The USB-C MacBook Neo has just the one data port, with the other reserved for charging. A dock with Power Delivery will greatly expand the entry-level Mac laptop.

For more detail, read our Thunderbolt 5 vs Thunderbolt 4 vs Thunderbolt 3 vs USB4 explainer.

Add external displays to your MacBook

If you use your laptop as your principal computer, attaching at least one larger display to create a hybrid desktop/laptop setup, with a keyboard and mouse, will boost your productivity. You can turn that 13in MacBook’s cramped screen real-estate into an iconic iMac-sized 27in or even larger screen by adding an extra display—or connect two or even four large monitors to extend your screen across your whole desk.

Take a look at our recommended best monitors and displays for Mac and also the best portable monitors for Mac.

You’ll get two or more Extended mode screens (where the screen extends beyond what you can see on the laptop screen) using a Thunderbolt connection (or DisplayPort/HDMI).

Natively over mere USB-C, Macs can connect to only one external display in Extended mode, as opposed to Mirrored mode (which replicates exactly what you get on the laptop screen) but DisplayLink is third-party software that allows some docks to extend to up to four screens on even the most basic Mac.

DisplayLink-supporting docks are also the only way that non-Pro/Max M1 and M2 MacBooks can connect more than one external display.

articles.title: The Utility App Flood Won’t Last
articles.subtitle: The App Store is evolving at a breakneck pace not seen since its earliest days. We saw the first glimmers of what was to come early in 2025, but it wasn’t until late last year that the tsunami of apps developed with the help of AI agents really took hold.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
The App Store is evolving at a breakneck pace not seen since its earliest days. We saw the first glimmers of what was to come early in 2025, but it wasn’t until late last year that the tsunami of apps developed with the help of AI agents really took hold.

Since then, veteran developers are releasing new apps and updating existing ones faster than ever, and new developers are releasing their first apps in droves. Today, supply is dramatically up, demand is flat, and quality is seemingly simultaneously up and down, depending on where you look.

How these forces play out long-term is anyone’s guess, but it’s worth examining because, just as Federico’s link to Bryan Irace’s post about agentic coding tools foreshadowed the rise of tools like Codex and Claude Code, today’s trends are sparks that have the potential to become tomorrow’s App Store wildfires or simply fizzle out.

Utility apps are on the front lines of this change. The TechCrunch story I linked in April picked up on this trend:

Another interesting tidbit from Appfigures is that the Utilities app category moved up the top five chart.

If anything, the trend has accelerated in the months since.

It’s not surprising at all that utility apps have taken off. They’ve been a staple of new developers since long before agents came along. That’s because many are UI wrappers around command line tools. That isn’t a knock against the developers of those apps; most users don’t want to open Terminal to convert a video or audio file to another format using ffmpeg, for example. By building a great UI around command line tools, developers have made them far easier to use.

However, the relative simplicity and narrow scope of many utility apps have made them a natural fit for AI agents, too. That’s why the App Store (and my inbox) is deluged with Mac menu bar and single-screen iPhone and iPad utility apps.

On the one hand, the abundance of utilities has been great for users. More choice means you’re more likely to find the app that perfectly fits your needs.

On the other hand, though, I don’t think what’s happening in the category is sustainable and expect to see it dramatically shift again in the coming months. As we’ve seen from reporting by The New York Times, app supply is outstripping demand by orders of magnitude, which will drive down prices. That alone is likely to cause the utility app market to shrink. But there’s more to it than that.

Remember, the demand shifts that The New York Times reported, based on Sensor Tower numbers, are for the entire App Store, where download numbers have grown 2-3% this year and last. I expect utility downloads to actually shrink in the coming months – again, because of agents.

Utilities, especially simple ones, are exactly the sorts of apps that are becoming trivially easy for power users – the very users these utilities are made for – to create themselves. From frontier labs‘ model improvements to a growing number of app-building tools from those same labs and third parties, it’s never been easier to build a web or native app yourself.

And although I agree with people, like Nilay Patel, who say the notion that everyone will build their own software is overblown, the utility market is different. Your average person is not downloading apps to adjust the frame rate and file format of a video or downloading YouTube videos to watch later.

But those are exactly the sort of things that people who are using agents are doing with them, whether they’re having an agent do those things directly via a command line tool in an app like Codex or Claude Code or building an app to do the same thing. That’s going to put even more pressure on the category.

That said, I think there will always be a cohort of users who would rather pay for an app than build it themselves, so I’m not predicting the demise of utilities in general – just the end of today’s frothy market. I also think there remains a place for simple utilities that solve hard problems with clever solutions. Not every utility is a UI wrapper for a terminal command. Plenty of apps feature original solutions or thoughtful and unconventional remixes of disparate tools.

Utilities aren’t going away, but just like other App Store deluges, the trend will recede. It’s just that this time, it’s likely to flip faster than usual.

articles.subtitle: Ubisoft have done the sensible thing and turned Rainbow Six into a turn-based tactical game. Nabbing the special ability-laden operators of Rainbow Six Siege and dropping them into the XCOM: Chimera Squad framework.
articles.author: Rock Paper Shotgun
articles.content:
Ubisoft have done the sensible thing and turned Rainbow Six into a turn-based tactical game. Nabbing the special ability-laden operators of Rainbow Six Siege and dropping them into the XCOM: Chimera Squad framework. The Mario + Rabbids developer have found a spin off that looks to be a natural fit for the series.

In Rainbow Six Tactics, you'll be returning to the tactical shoes of Paul Bishop, protagonist of Rainbow Six Vegas 1 and 2. Though he has now hung up his flashbang belt and rappel rope and settled into the Rainbow commander's chair. It's a tense time in the control room as a terrorist group has started launching attacks around the globe and, wouldn't you know it, Rainbow are the only international team of super agents who can put the trouble down.

Rather than starting with blank slate cadets and specialising them through combat, as in full-fat XCOM, Rainbow Six Tactics is more similar to XCOM spin-off Chimera Squad or Tactical Breach Wizards, where you have a set roster of operators who each come equipped with special abilities. Though, naturally, this makes sense for Ubisoft's take on the genre, as all of its 15 operators are pulled from Rainbow Six Siege and bring with them their abilities from the 5v5 hero shooter.

Watching through the trailer, I clocked Nokk, Glaz, Montagne, Ash, Doc, Sledge, and Zofia, so there will be a good spread of aggressive damage dealers, support units, flankers, and snipers. It also plays well into the destructible environments, with certain characters, such as Sledge, very capable of breaking through walls to open up paths through a level.

Another lift from Rainbow Six Siege is the reconnaissance phase that starts each mission. Before you get into the action of Rainbow Six Tactics, you use drones to eye up the map and spot where terrorists are hiding in the level. While Ubisoft's levels aren't procedurally generated, like those in XCOM 2, enemy spawn positions will change each time you play, so that reconnaissance phase will be useful.

There is one last step before the action kicks off proper: breaching. Each map has several breach points, so depending on what you find on the other side of the wall in the reconnaissance phase, different breach points will be more tempting. Pick a point and watch your four chosen operators stack up on a wall, blast their way inside a locked room, and work together to shoot any immediate targets. After which the action switches to more traditional turn-based play.

I play a lot of turn-based tactical games and, as I've tried to show above, Rainbow Six Tactics features a lot of mechanics from other games in the genre. XCOM: Chimera Squad, Tactical Breach Wizards, a smidge of Door Kickers. That said, that cribbing hasn't soured me in Rainbow Six Tactics, they're all natural touchstones for a turn-based take on Siege, and none of the games Ubisoft are pulling from combine these features in quite this way.

The element of Siege that is on show in the trailer, but I want to see more of in action is destructible environments. It's such a central pillar to Rainbow Six Siege that I'd hope it was brought over with a similar level of care and thought. Yes, in Siege, destruction is used to open up new pathways through a level, but it is also a vital tool for intel gathering.

Knocking a small hole in a wall lets you see through into a room or corridor beyond. The recon phase in Rainbow Six Tactics suggests the challenge of fog of war, and so something of that use for destruction could live in the turn-based game, but I'd like to see more to know for sure.

Rainbow Six Tactics isn't due out until 2027, so there's a bit of a wait. But, I'm also heartened to see there is non-Siege life in the series. After all, this is the first single-player Rainbow Six game since (the excellent) Vegas 2, 17 years ago.

articles.title: MacPaw is building an on-device AI layer that will work across your Mac apps
articles.subtitle: MacPaw has announced a long-term strategic partnership with Liquid AI to co-develop an on-device AI technology stack built specifically for the Mac. The collaboration will start with Eney, MacPaw’s AI assistant for macOS.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
MacPaw has announced a long-term strategic partnership with Liquid AI to co-develop an on-device AI technology stack built specifically for the Mac.

The collaboration will start with Eney, MacPaw’s AI assistant for macOS.

MacPaw is teaming up with Liquid AI to bring more on-device AI to the Mac

Liquid AI’s Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs) will be adapted for Mac-based assistance and combined with MacPaw’s own on-device technologies: Mnemos for memory and Elix for inference.

Eney already shifted to a local model last year, keeping reasoning, contextual search, skill execution, and conversation history on the device whenever possible.

The new partnership is intended to push that approach further. The two companies are jointly developing the underlying stack rather than MacPaw simply adding another third-party model.

Once the technology has been tested and implemented in Eney, MacPaw says it plans to bring it to more of its products. It also wants to make the shared AI stack available to Mac developers through Setapp.

That could let participating apps expose more of their capabilities and context to Eney. This would allow the assistant to understand what is inside an app. It could also provide more useful answers or take relevant actions.

You can learn more about MacPaw’s on-device AI technology and today’s announcement here, and catch up on Liquid AI here.
